newsitem.title: BULGARIA: NO QUICK FIX FOR BULGARIAN ECONOMY, OECD WARNS.
newsitem.headline: NO QUICK FIX FOR BULGARIAN ECONOMY, OECD WARNS.

text.p: Bulgaria's economy needs a
comprehensive programme of macroeconomic and structural reform
and a currency board is only part of the solution, the
Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development said.
In its first report on Bulgaria, it said the fixed exchange
rate mechanism proposed by the IMF must be accompanied by
measures to address problems in the banking sector, enterprise
restructuring, and fiscal imbalances.
"As the macroeconomic instability in Bulgaria has
structural roots, any programme aimed at macroeconomic
stabilisation that does not involve simultaneous measures to
deal with loss-making firms and insolvent or undercapitalised
commercial banks is bound for failure," the OECD said.
The OECD forecast that non-member Bulgaria's GDP would
shrink by six percent in 1997 but said its projections
especially for inflation and the government budget would depend
greatly on if and when a currency board was introduced.
A currency board strictly matches local currency in
circulation to central bank reserves, effectively pegging the
local currency to a foreign currency and severely restricting
government fiscal activity with the aim of restoring confidence
and reducing high inflation.
The OECD survey was drawn up late last year before the
Socialist government was ousted by mass protests and the
interim government negotiated a standby agreement with the IMF.
The currency board is expected to be introduced in June.
As commercial banks would lose access to refinancing under
a currency board, the OECD recommended measures to limit the
number of operating banks, recapitalise them, and step up
monitoring of their activities.
The report said the government must continue isolating and
closing the most problematic loss-making state enterprises, to
prevent a further increase in inter-enterprise debt.
Under a currency board, the government would no longer be
able to borrow from the central bank to finance the budget
deficit, and would initially need funds from external sources
or privatisation revenue.
However, the OECD said the restoration of confidence in the
lev would alleviate fiscal problems, as lower interest rates
would decrease the burden of debt service and possibilities for
placing state securities with private foreign and domestic
investors would grow.
The OECD said reforms would need a major commitment both
from the Bulgarian authorities and the international community.
The standby accord goes to the IMF board for approval later
this month, and the G-24 industrialised nations meet in
Brussels next week to discuss additional support.
"Strong social and political pressures will need to be
resisted in order to maintain financial discipline and
control," the OECD warned.
The OECD recommended that the government should encourage
expansion of the activities of foreign banks in Bulgaria, which
could provide human capital and supply some liquidity to the
interbank loans market to ease the strain from limited central
bank refinancing.
They would be able to provide some commercial credit to
firms, and would possess the liquidity to absorb some state
securities used to finance the budget deficit.
The OECD said tax reform should concentrate on greater
stability and enforcement of lower, uniformly applicable rates,
to reduce the current levels of evasion and improve revenues.
It said the government needed to streamline foreign
investment procedures and continue to speed up privatisation.
The OECD warned that the currency board was "in no sense a
quick fix; it is an approach that will have to be persevered
with in the face of possibly heavy adjustment costs.
